title: Legendre Transformation
notes: Open by naming the central move: a point x on a smooth convex graph is replaced by its slope p. The Legendre transform is not a new curve drawn from nowhere; it is the same supporting-tangent information written in slope coordinates. Keep the tangent line visible because it carries both the value of the conjugate and the equality case in Fenchel's inequality.

title: Slope Coordinates
notes: The first technical habit is to stop treating p as a mysterious dual variable. For a differentiable convex function, p is the gradient at x. When strict convexity removes flat segments, the slope changes injectively with x; when essential smoothness controls the boundary, the slope map behaves like a coordinate chart rather than a partial label.

title: Tangent Line Intercept
notes: Use the tangent line as the visual definition. At a paired point, the tangent has equation t(z)=p z minus f star of p. Rearranging the tangent formula gives f star of p equals p x minus f of x. This is exactly the affine gap that the conjugate maximizes, but here it is attained by the slope-matched point.

title: Conjugate As Transformed Graph
notes: This slide turns the graph into data. Starting with x, compute p as the gradient and then compute the intercept ledger value f star of p. The point on the dual graph is therefore produced by a parametrized transformation from the primal graph. Fenchel equality is the checksum that the pair has not drifted apart.

title: Gradient Map
notes: Connect the picture to the source-span theorem language. A closed proper convex function has a single-valued subdifferential exactly in the essentially smooth case. On the interior of the effective domain that single value is the gradient. The gradient map is therefore the ordinary-function version of the subdifferential map.

title: Inverse Gradient
notes: Now add the symmetry. If both sides have the right smooth and strict-convex behavior, the conjugate gradient sends p back to the original x. Students should say this aloud as a coordinate statement: primal position maps to slope, and slope maps back to primal position. The conjugate is smooth because the inverse map is well behaved on its natural domain.

title: Quadratic Example
notes: The quadratic is the calibration example because every line can be checked mentally. If f of x is x squared, the slope is p equals two x, the inverse is x equals p over two, and the dual value is p squared over four. The shape comparison shows the reciprocal curvature idea before any matrix notation appears.

title: Entropy And Barrier Examples
notes: Use these one-dimensional examples to show why domains matter. Entropy sends positive x to every real slope, while the log barrier sends positive x only to negative slopes. Both are smooth inside their domains and both have gradients that blow up at the boundary, but their slope ranges lead to different conjugate domains.

title: Hessian Reciprocity
notes: Differentiate the inverse-gradient identity rather than memorizing a new formula. If p equals grad f of x and x equals grad f star of p, then the derivative of one map is the inverse derivative of the other. In one dimension this says the two second derivatives multiply to one at paired points.

title: Domain And Range Caveats
notes: Pause on the warning because it prevents overgeneralization. The Legendre conjugate first lives on the image of the gradient map, not automatically on all of dual space. Without the boundary blow-up and strictness hypotheses, the image may fail to be an open convex coordinate domain, so the ordinary conjugate needs a closure-and-extension step.

title: Numerical Legendre Lab
notes: Treat the lab as a small instrument panel. The equality rows test slope-matched pairs, the off-slope rows test nonnegative Fenchel gaps, and the round-trip residual tests gradient inversion. The numbers are not the proof, but they make the proof obligations inspectable and catch the common mistake of pairing x with the wrong slope.

title: Rule Ledger
notes: This ledger is a memory aid for the section. Essential smoothness makes the subdifferential single-valued, essential strict convexity is dual to essential smoothness, Legendre type makes the transform symmetric between interiors, and strict plus co-finite finite functions give the full-space version where the classical transformation and Fenchel conjugacy coincide.

title: Boundary And Closure
notes: After computing the Legendre conjugate on the slope range, the ordinary conjugate may still require boundary values and infinity outside the closure of the range. This is a source of many wrong answers: a formula obtained by inverting the gradient is only the interior chart unless the hypotheses guarantee that the chart already covers the full relevant domain.

title: Recap
notes: Close by asking students to narrate the whole loop. Start from x, compute p by the gradient, write the tangent line, record f star of p, verify Fenchel equality, invert by grad f star, and compare Hessians. That loop is the Legendre transformation as smooth conjugacy through slope coordinates.
